explain.say: Leave milk or meat out of the fridge and in a day or two it smells bad, tastes sour or turns slimy. Food goes off because tiny living things are eating it before you do.

explain.say: Bacteria, yeasts and mould spores are on our hands, in the air and on the food itself. Food is perfect for them, full of water and nutrients.

explain.say: In the warmth, some bacteria can split in two every 20 to 30 minutes, so a few become millions in hours. A fridge keeps them cold and slow; a freezer stops them growing altogether.

explain.say: As they feed, microbes give off waste: acids that turn milk sour, smelly gases and slime. The food's own enzymes and the air also break it down, turning bananas brown and fats rancid.

faq.q: Where do the germs on food come from?
faq.a: Microbes are almost everywhere: in soil, air and water, on animals, on our hands and on food as it is picked or made. Clean hands and kitchens keep the starting number low.
asks: How do bacteria get on food?

faq.q: Why does a fridge keep food fresh?
faq.a: Cold slows microbes down. Below about 5 degrees Celsius most bacteria grow very slowly, and in a freezer they stop growing, though most are not killed and wake up when thawed.
Bacteria in milk feed on its sugar, lactose, and turn it into lactic acid. The acid makes the milk taste sour and makes its proteins clump into lumps.
asks: Why does old milk go lumpy?

faq.q: Can you tell food is unsafe by smelling it?
faq.a: Not always. The bacteria that make food smell bad are often different from those that cause food poisoning, which can grow without changing the smell or taste. Follow use-by dates.
asks: Is it safe if it smells fine?

faq.q: How do people stop food going off?
faq.a: By making life hard for microbes: cooling, freezing, drying, salting, adding sugar or vinegar, heating in sealed cans, or fermenting with friendly microbes that crowd out harmful ones.
asks: How was food kept before fridges?

facts: Some bacteria can divide about every 20 minutes in ideal conditions.
Bacteria grow fastest between about 5 and 60 degrees Celsius, a range food safety experts call the danger zone.
Freezing stops bacteria growing but does not kill most of them.
